header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE.
Dr. Talha Muadh Ghulam Jilani, etc.
J U D G M E N T.
body: Date of hearing: 19.11.2026.
Petitioners by: Mr. Bilal Awais, Advocate.
Federation by: Rana Arfan Ali, Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan.
Respondent-NADRA by: Mr. Mehar Din Mazari, Advocate.

MUHAMMAD AJMAL ZAHID, J. Through this Constitutional Petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 ("the Constitution"), the petitioners seek a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to issue a Pakistan Origin Card ("POC") to petitioner No.1, an American citizen of Indian origin, on the basis of his marriage to petitioner No.2, a citizen of Pakistan. The controversy essentially concerns the scope of eligibility under Rule 4(5) of the National Database and Registration Authority (Pakistan Origin Card) Rules, 2002 ("the Rules"), the effect of the prescribed security-verification mechanism and the nature and extent of the discretion vested in the Federal Government under the third proviso to the said Rule.

2. Briefly, the facts giving rise to the instant petition are that petitioner No.1 claims to be an American citizen of Indian origin and is married to petitioner No.2, a Pakistani citizen. Both petitioners are stated to be residing in Pakistan. According to petitioner No.1, he embraced Islam in 1990 and, consequent thereto, changed his name W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 2 from Dr. Jaysinha Shamrao Shinde to Dr. Talha Muadh Ghulam Jilani. He further claims to have renounced his Indian nationality before acquiring American citizenship in 2007. According to the petitioners, on 26.05.2021, petitioner No.1 submitted an application for issuance of a POC. Initially, respondent No.3 declined to entertain the application on the ground of his Indian origin; however, subsequently, certain particulars were sought for verification. Through an email dated 14.01.2022, petitioner No.1 was informed that his case had been referred to the concerned authorities for ground verification. Having failed to obtain the desired relief from the Federal Ombudsman, the petitioners approached this Court through W.P. No.65658/2022. Vide order dated 24.10.2022, the matter was referred to the Chairman, NADRA, for consideration. The representation submitted pursuant thereto was rejected vide order dated 27.01.2023. Thereafter, petitioner No.1 approached respondent No.2, the Secretary, Ministry of Interior, invoking the third proviso to Rule 4(5) of the Rules and seeking relaxation in his favour. Pursuant to the directions issued by this Court in W.P. No.46874/2023 vide order dated 16.02.2023 and the subsequent contempt proceedings, the matter was considered by the competent authority. However, the request was declined through the impugned report dated 28.03.2024 and order dated 25.06.2024. Hence, the instant petition.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that petitioner No.1, being married to a Pakistani citizen, squarely falls within the ambit of Rule 4(5) of the Rules and is, therefore, legally entitled to obtain a POC. It is argued that his acquisition of American citizenship and renunciation of Indian nationality remove any disqualification that could otherwise arise from his former nationality. The respondents, according to learned counsel, have unlawfully treated his Indian origin as an absolute bar, although the Rules do not prescribe any independent disqualification merely on the basis of ethnic or ancestral origin. It is further contended that the policy dated 02.04.2013, requiring security clearance from ISI and W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 3 IB in respect of applicants belonging to List-B countries, cannot override the statutory Rules or introduce an additional condition of eligibility. Learned counsel maintains that the third proviso to Rule 4(5) confers a statutory power of relaxation which was not exercised fairly, objectively or in accordance with law. Reliance is also placed upon Article 35 of the Constitution, which obligates the State to protect marriage and family, and it is urged that refusal to issue a POC adversely affects the petitioners' legitimate interest in maintaining their matrimonial and family life in Pakistan. On these premises, the impugned decisions are assailed as arbitrary, discriminatory and without lawful authority.

4. Conversely, learned law officer for the respondents supports the impugned decisions and submits that the petitioner's matrimonial relationship with a Pakistani citizen does not dispense with the security-verification requirements prescribed under the Rules. It is contended that the application was duly processed and referred to the competent security agencies, but the requisite favourable clearance was not forthcoming from both agencies. The policy dated 02.04.2013, according to the respondents, provides a uniform mechanism for enhanced scrutiny of applicants belonging to List-B countries, including India and Afghanistan, in view of legitimate national-security considerations. It is further submitted that the third proviso to Rule 4(5) vests discretion in the Federal Government, which cannot be claimed as an enforceable right by an applicant. The respondents, therefore, maintain that the impugned decisions have been taken in accordance with law and do not warrant interference in constitutional jurisdiction.

5. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and examining the available record, the following questions arise for determination: I. Whether marriage to a Pakistani citizen under Rule 4(5) of the Rules creates an indefeasible right to issuance of a POC, irrespective of the prescribed verification and security requirements?

II. Whether the Ministry of Interior policy dated 02.04.2013, requiring security clearance from ISI and IB in respect of W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 4 applicants belonging to List-B countries, is legally sustainable and capable of being applied to the petitioner's case?

III. Whether the third proviso to Rule 4(5) confers an enforceable right to relaxation upon an otherwise ineligible applicant, or merely vests a discretionary power in the Federal Government, subject to judicial review?

IV. Whether this Court, while exercising jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution, can substitute its own assessment for that of the competent security agencies? V. Whether Article 35 of the Constitution confers an enforceable right to issuance of a POC, overriding the statutory requirements governing registration and issuance thereof?

6. Before examining the controversy, it is necessary to advert to the statutory framework governing the issuance of a POC. Section 11 of the National Database and Registration Authority Ordinance, 2000 ("the Ordinance") empowers NADRA to issue or renew POCs to such prescribed classes of foreigners and citizens having dual nationality as may be determined in accordance with the prescribed criteria, terms and conditions. The Rules framed thereunder provide the mechanism for determining eligibility, registration, verification and issuance of the card. The rights and privileges attached to a POC, as well as the conditions subject to which it may be issued and retained, must consequently be determined within the four corners of the Ordinance and the Rules.

7. In "Regional Manager, NADRA RHO, Hayatabad, Peshawar and another v. Mst. Hajira and another" (2024 SCMR 197 = 2023 SCP 377), the Hon'ble Supreme Court emphasized that NADRA, being a statutory authority, is obliged to act in accordance with its governing law and should not compel applicants to initiate unnecessary litigation by failing to discharge its statutory obligations. Similarly, in "Muhammad Ibrahim Shaikh v. Government of Pakistan (PLD 2019 SC 133), the Hon'ble Supreme Court examined the statutory framework governing POCs, including the eligibility provisions contained in Rules 2, 3, 4 and 5 and the benefits available W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 5 to holders of such cards under Rule 17. These pronouncements establish that the issuance and regulation of POCs are governed by the Ordinance and the Rules. Neither the Authority nor an applicant can claim a right or exercise a power divorced from the statutory framework.

8. A POC is not equivalent to Pakistani citizenship, nor does its issuance confer citizenship upon its holder. It is an identity and facilitation document issued to foreigners falling within the classes recognized under the Rules, carrying the rights and benefits specified therein. Its issuance is, therefore, subject to the statutory qualifications, conditions and restrictions prescribed by law and cannot be claimed as an unconditional or absolute right merely on the basis of a matrimonial relationship with a Pakistani citizen.

9. Rule 4(5) of the Rules recognizes a foreigner married to a citizen of Pakistan as an eligible foreigner of Pakistan origin for so long as the marriage subsists, subject to the provisos appended thereto. The second proviso excludes a foreign spouse who is a citizen or national of India, a state or country not recognized by Pakistan, or an enemy country. The third proviso, however, empowers the Federal Government, in special and extraordinary circumstances and upon an application made by the concerned person, to allow a foreigner otherwise ineligible under the second proviso to be registered and issued a POC. Thus, the Rule creates a category of eligibility based on marriage, while simultaneously prescribing certain exclusions and providing a limited mechanism for relaxation in exceptional circumstances.

10. Rule 9 authorizes NADRA to conduct such inquiry and require such documentary or other evidence as may be considered necessary to ascertain an applicant's eligibility and compliance with the applicable requirements. Rule 10 provides for issuance of a card to a person duly registered in accordance with the Rules. Furthermore, Rule 13 empowers the Authority, notwithstanding an applicant's otherwise established eligibility, to refuse registration or issuance of a card where, in its opinion, such registration or issuance W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 6 would be prejudicial to the sovereignty, integrity, security or defence of Pakistan, its friendly relations with foreign states, maintenance of law and order or public interest.

11. A harmonious reading of these provisions demonstrates that eligibility under Rule 4(5), verification under Rule 9 and the power of refusal under Rule 13 operate in distinct but complementary fields. Marriage to a Pakistani citizen may establish the threshold eligibility contemplated by Rule 4(5), but it does not render the remaining statutory requirements redundant or extinguish the Authority's power to refuse registration or issuance on the grounds recognized under Rule 13. In other words, eligibility is a necessary statutory condition for obtaining a POC, but it is not, by itself, sufficient to compel its issuance irrespective of the other requirements of the Rules.

12. In the present case, petitioner No.1 admittedly traces his origin to India. He asserts that he renounced Indian nationality before acquiring American citizenship in 2007. Although, the petitioners have annexed a certificate purportedly evidencing renunciation of Indian nationality, however, this Court has neither been provided with any independent verification of its genuineness nor has any material been placed before it to establish that the competent authorities have accepted the cessation of his former nationality. The authenticity and legal effect of a document issued by a foreign authority cannot be conclusively determined merely on the basis of its production before this Court, particularly where the matter is subject to verification by the competent authorities.

13. At this stage, it is imperative to distinguish between Indian origin and Indian nationality. The second proviso to Rule 4(5), as applicable to the controversy, speaks of a person being a citizen or national of India; it does not, in terms, impose an independent disqualification merely on account of Indian ancestry or ethnic origin. Consequently, the petitioner's Indian origin, by itself, cannot be treated as conclusive proof that he continues to be an Indian citizen or national. Conversely, his assertion that he renounced Indian nationality and subsequently acquired American citizenship does not, W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 7 without satisfactory verification and supporting material, conclusively establish the cessation of his former nationality for the purposes of the Rules. The distinction is material because statutory eligibility must be determined on the basis of the legal status prescribed by the Rules and not merely by reference to ethnic origin, ancestry or an unverified assertion regarding nationality.

14. The next aspect concerns the policy dated 02.04.2013 issued by the Ministry of Interior, whereby applicants belonging to List-B countries, including India and Afghanistan, are subjected to enhanced security scrutiny and their applications are processed after obtaining favourable recommendations from ISI and IB. Admittedly, the said policy is an executive instruction and cannot override the statutory Rules or create an independent disqualification not contemplated therein. Nor can it amend the statutory criteria of eligibility prescribed under Rule 4(5). Nevertheless, the policy may legitimately provide an administrative mechanism for enhanced security verification, keeping in view the State's responsibility to safeguard its sovereignty, integrity, security and defence. Its validity, therefore, lies in its operation as a mechanism of scrutiny and verification, and not as an independent source of disqualification.

15. This Court, while exercising constitutional jurisdiction, does not ordinarily sit in appeal over policy decisions of the executive, particularly those involving national security, unless such decisions are shown to be unconstitutional, arbitrary, discriminatory, mala fide or otherwise contrary to law. The policy dated 02.04.2013 has not been shown to suffer from any such infirmity. The requirement of enhanced security scrutiny for applicants belonging to specified countries has a rational nexus with the legitimate object of protecting national security. However, such policy cannot be applied mechanically or in a manner that supplants the statutory framework. Its application must remain subject to the governing law and the decision ultimately taken by the competent statutory authority. Reliance in this regard is placed upon the case titled "Vice- Chancellor, Agriculture University, Peshawar and others v. W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 8 Muhammad Shafiq and others" (2024 SCMR 527), wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that policy formulation ordinarily falls within the domain and prerogative of the Executive and that Courts should refrain from interfering in institutional policy decisions in the absence of a violation of fundamental rights or any other recognized ground of judicial review. The aforesaid principle, however, does not place executive policy beyond judicial scrutiny. The Court retains the jurisdiction to examine whether the policy is consistent with the governing statute and whether its application in an individual case is lawful, reasonable and non-arbitrary.

16. In "Wukala Mahaz Barai Tahafaz Dastoor v. Federation of Pakistan and another" (2014 SCMR 111), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while dealing with matters relating to foreign policy, national defence and security, emphasized the limits of judicial interference in matters falling within the executive domain and observed that judicial intervention in such matters may offend the constitutional principle of trichotomy of powers. The principle enunciated therein requires due judicial restraint in matters of national security. It does not, however, extinguish the constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court to examine whether an action taken by a public authority is within its lawful authority, is founded upon relevant considerations and is free from mala fides or arbitrariness. The Court is not required to undertake an independent assessment of intelligence material, but neither is it obliged to accept every administrative assertion of national security without examining the legality of the decisionmaking process.

17. In the present case, the respondents have maintained that the petitioner's application was referred to the competent security agencies and that the requisite favourable recommendations were not forthcoming from both agencies. Such recommendations, being part of the prescribed security-verification mechanism, constitute a relevant consideration in processing the application. A matrimonial relationship with a Pakistani citizen cannot, by itself, neutralize W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 9 legitimate security concerns or dispense with the verification required under the applicable statutory framework.

18. It is, nevertheless, necessary to emphasize that an adverse or unavailable security recommendation cannot, by itself, be treated as an automatic statutory disqualification under Rule 4(5), nor can the policy dated 02.04.2013 substitute the satisfaction required under Rule 13. The competent authority must independently consider the material available to it and form an opinion, in accordance with law, as to whether issuance of the POC would attract any of the grounds specified in Rule 13. The security agencies provide relevant input; the statutory decision must ultimately be that of the authority upon which the Rules confer the power. In the present case, the petitioners have not demonstrated that the competent authority acted without jurisdiction, mechanically adopted an extraneous consideration as a substitute for the statutory requirements, or reached its conclusion through mala fide exercise of power. Nor have they placed any material before this Court to establish that the impugned decision is founded upon Indian origin alone, rather than the securityverification process undertaken in accordance with the applicable framework.

19. The petitioners' reliance upon the third proviso to Rule 4(5) also requires consideration. The said proviso empowers the Federal Government, in special and extraordinary circumstances and upon an application made by the concerned person, to allow registration and issuance of a POC to a foreigner otherwise rendered ineligible under the second proviso. The language employed in the provision makes it clear that the power is discretionary and is intended to operate in exceptional circumstances. The use of the expression "may" does not confer an automatic or vested right upon an applicant to obtain relaxation. Equally, however, the provision does not authorize an arbitrary or mechanical refusal. An applicant is entitled to have his request considered by the competent authority in accordance with the statutory purpose, upon relevant considerations and through a lawful exercise of discretion. Mere marriage to a Pakistani citizen, without W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 10 establishing circumstances of a special and extraordinary nature warranting relaxation, does not ipso facto compel the Federal Government to exercise the power in the applicant's favour.

20. It is equally well settled that statutory discretion, though vested in the competent authority, is not unfettered and must be exercised within the limits and for the purposes for which it has been conferred. In "Federation of Pakistan v. Muhammad Saifullah Khan (PLD 1989 SC 166), the Hon'ble Supreme Court recognized that a discretionary power must be exercised in good faith and in accordance with the object of the law. The exercise of discretion must be fair, reasonable, transparent and impartial, and must not be arbitrary, capricious, mala fide or based upon irrelevant considerations. Reliance in this regard is further placed upon "Commissioner Inland Revenue, Karachi v. Pakistan Beverages Limited, Karachi (2018 SCMR 1544); Human Rights Case No.3654 of 2018 (In the matter regarding appointment of Managing Director/Chairman, Pakistan Television Corporation) (2019 SCMR 1); Aman Ullah Khan and others v. The Federal Government of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Islamabad and others (PLD 1990 SC 1092); Government of N.-W.F.P. through Secretary and 3 others v. Mejee Flour (1997 SCMR 1804, at page 1810-D); Tariq Aziz-ud-Din and others (2010 SCMR 1301); Abu Bakar Siddique and others v. Collector of Customs, Lahore and others (2006 SCMR 705, at page 716-H); Corruption in Hajj Arrangements in 2010 (PLD 2011 SC 963); Pir Imran Sajid v. Managing Director/General Manager (Manager Finance), Telephone Industries of Pakistan (2015 SCMR 1257); Muhammad Amin Muhammad Bashir Limited v. Government of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Islamabad and others (2015 PTD 1100); Lahore Development Authority through Director General and others v. Ms. Imrana Tiwana and others (2015 SCMR 1739, para 86); Independent Newspapers Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd. and another v. Chairman, Fourth Wage Board (1993 SCMR 1533); Habibullah Energy Limited and another v. WAPDA through Chairman and W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 11 others (PLD 2014 SC 47); Muhammad Ashraf Tiwana and others v. Pakistan and others (2013 SCMR 1159); Contempt Proceedings against Chief Secretary, Sindh and others (2013 SCMR 1752); Muhammad Zahir Raja v. Federation of Pakistan (2012 SCMR 971); Federation of Pakistan and others v. Messrs Charsadda Sugar Mills Limited (1978 SCMR 428); Samiullah Khan Marwat v. Government of Pakistan through Secretary Establishment, Islamabad and another (2003 SCMR 1140); Muhammad Hussain v. Dr. Zahoor Alam (2010 SCMR 286); Inspector-General (Prisons), N.-W.F.P., Peshawar v. Syed Jaffar Shah and others (2009 PLC (C.S.) 47); Syed Nasir Hussain Shah v. Zila Naib Nazim, Sukkur and 21 others (2008 SCMR 1650); Chairman, Regional Transport Authority, Rawalpindi v. Pakistan Mutual Insurance Company Limited (PLD 1991 SC 14); Abid Hassan v. P.I.A.C. (2005 PLC (C.S.) 1117); Walayat Ali Mir v. Pakistan International Airlines Corporation (1995 SCMR 650); M/s. Novitas International v. Income Tax Officer (Films Circle) and another (1991 PTD 968); Messrs Zeenat Manufacturing (Pvt.) Ltd., Gadoon Amazai Industrial Estate v. Central Board of Revenue (1999 SCMR 979); and Mayzone Pak. International v. Additional Secretary, Government of Pakistan (2002 CLC 388).

21. In the instant case, the petitioners have not identified any specific special or extraordinary circumstance, beyond the matrimonial relationship already recognized under Rule 4(5), which would demonstrate that the refusal of relaxation was arbitrary, irrational or founded upon an irrelevant consideration. The factum of marriage establishes the petitioner's claim to consideration under the relevant provision, but does not, without more, establish an exceptional circumstance compelling the Federal Government to exercise its relaxation power. The petitioners have also failed to demonstrate that the competent authority disregarded any mandatory statutory requirement, acted in bad faith or refused to consider the representation on its own merits. Consequently, no unlawful exercise of discretion under the third proviso has been established. W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 12 22. The scope of jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution also requires consideration. A writ of mandamus is issued to compel the performance of a public duty where the law imposes a corresponding obligation upon the public functionary. It cannot ordinarily be employed to compel an authority to exercise a discretionary power in a particular manner, particularly where the statute entrusts the ultimate decision to the satisfaction of the competent authority. The Court may, where warranted, require the authority to exercise its jurisdiction in accordance with law, but cannot ordinarily dictate the outcome of a decision which the legislature has entrusted to its discretion.

23. The jurisdiction under Article 199 is extraordinary and discretionary, intended to secure lawful administration and prevent injustice. It does not authorize the Court to substitute its own opinion for that of a statutory authority merely because another view may also be possible. Interference is warranted where the impugned action suffers from want of jurisdiction, violation of law, procedural illegality, arbitrariness, mala fides, reliance upon irrelevant considerations or disregard of mandatory legal requirements. The exercise of constitutional jurisdiction must, therefore, remain within the recognized limits of judicial review.

24. In matters involving security assessment, the distinction between judicial review and appellate reconsideration assumes particular significance. The Court may examine the legality of the decision-making process, the competence of the authority, the relevance of the considerations taken into account and whether the decision has a rational basis in the statutory framework. It may also intervene where the decision is shown to be mala fide, arbitrary or founded upon an unlawful criterion. It cannot, however, assume the functions of the security agencies or undertake an independent evaluation of intelligence inputs in order to arrive at its own security conclusion. Judicial restraint in such matters is dictated by institutional competence and the constitutional distribution of W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 13 functions, but it does not amount to abdication of the Court's power of judicial review.

25. Tested on the aforesaid principles, the petitioners have not established any jurisdictional defect, material procedural irregularity or mala fide exercise of authority warranting interference under Article 199 of the Constitution. The application was processed, the matter was referred for security verification and the petitioner's subsequent request for relaxation was placed before the competent authority. The mere disagreement of an applicant with the outcome of a security-verification process, without demonstrating any illegality in the decision-making process, does not render the resulting decision unlawful. No sufficient material has been placed before this Court to warrant substitution of its assessment for that of the competent authorities.

26. The petitioners have also invoked Article 35 of the Constitution, which requires the State to protect marriage, family, mother and child. There can be no cavil with the proposition that the Constitution recognizes the importance of marriage and family as fundamental social institutions and places a corresponding obligation upon the State to protect them. However, Article 35 forms part of the Principles of Policy contained in Chapter 2 of Part II of the Constitution. Article 30(2) expressly provides that the validity of an action or law cannot be called into question merely on the ground that it is inconsistent with the Principles of Policy and that such principles are not enforceable by any Court.

27. Article 35, therefore, does not independently confer an automatic or directly enforceable right to issuance of a POC, nor does it dispense with the statutory conditions governing registration and issuance of such a card. It cannot be construed as overriding the express provisions of the Ordinance and the Rules or as compelling the competent authority to disregard legitimate national-security considerations.

28. This, however, does not mean that the matrimonial relationship or the legitimate interest of the petitioners in W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 14 maintaining their family unity may be disregarded by the State. Such considerations are relevant and deserve due weight in the administration of the statutory framework, particularly where the Rules themselves recognize a foreign spouse of a Pakistani citizen as an eligible category. Nevertheless, the constitutional importance of family life cannot be construed as an overriding entitlement to obtain an identity document in disregard of the applicable law and legitimate national-security requirements.

29. The legislature has expressly recognized the position of foreign spouses through Rule 4(5), while simultaneously preserving the powers of inquiry, verification and refusal under the other provisions of the Rules. These provisions must be read harmoniously so that effect is given to each of them. The petitioner's marriage to a Pakistani citizen is, therefore, a relevant statutory consideration and brings his case within the category contemplated by Rule 4(5), subject to the applicable provisos. It does not, however, extinguish the Authority's power to undertake verification or to refuse registration or issuance where the statutory grounds are lawfully attracted.

30. The respondents' actions must ultimately be examined against the requirements of the governing statutory framework. The record demonstrates that the petitioner's application was entertained, particulars were sought, the matter was referred for verification and the subsequent representation before the competent authority was considered. The impugned report dated 28.03.2024 and order dated 25.06.2024 disclose the basis upon which the request was declined. The petitioners have not been able to establish that the competent authority was not legally empowered to consider the matter or that the process adopted was contrary to the applicable Rules.

31. The petitioners have, therefore, failed to establish that the respondents acted without jurisdiction, applied an unlawful absolute bar on the basis of Indian origin, treated the executive policy as an independent statutory disqualification, or exercised their discretion arbitrarily or in bad faith. Equally, no material has been brought on W.P. No.24936 of 2025. 15 record to demonstrate that the competent authority failed to consider the request for relaxation in accordance with the third proviso to Rule 4(5). In these circumstances, the impugned decisions do not call for interference in the extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction of this Court.

32. For the foregoing reasons, the questions formulated above are answered accordingly. It is held that marriage to a Pakistani citizen under Rule 4(5) of the Rules does not, by itself, create an indefeasible right to issuance of a POC irrespective of the applicable verification and security requirements. Equally, Indian origin cannot, by itself, be treated as conclusive proof of Indian nationality or as an independent statutory disqualification under the second proviso to Rule 4(5). The policy dated 02.04.2013 may operate as a mechanism for enhanced security scrutiny, but cannot override the statutory Rules or replace the satisfaction required under Rule 12. The discretion vested in the Federal Government under the third proviso to Rule 4(5) is subject to judicial review on recognized grounds of illegality, arbitrariness and mala fides, but relaxation cannot be claimed as a matter of right. Similarly, Article 35, while underscoring the constitutional importance of family unity, does not override the statutory conditions governing issuance of a POC. On the facts and material placed before this Court, the petitioners have failed to establish any legally sustainable ground warranting issuance of the writ sought.
33. As an inevitable corollary of above discussion, this Constitutional Petition, being devoid of merit, force and substance, is dismissed.
(MUHAMMAD AJMAL ZAHID)
JUDGE.
Approved for Reporting.
